items.title: [ScienceDaily] A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

items.title: [Reason] Age-Related Synaptic Dysfunction and Possible Approaches to Treatment
items.content_html: Dysfunction of the synaptic connections between neurons in the brain is characteristic of aging and exaggerated in neurodegenerative conditions, particularly Alzheimer's disease. The brain is a collection of neural networks: a neuron extends branching axons that connect to other neurons via synapse structures. When synapses lose function, the network loses function, and cognitive decline is the result. Here, researchers discuss the biochemistry of synapses and a variety of approaches to therapy that might improve matters. They conclude that the most promising approaches at the present time are those focused on reducing the impact of aging on the function of glial cells. Glia in the brain (microglia, astrocytes, and so forth) support the function of neural networks in a broad variety of ways, and their progressive […]

items.title: [ecdc.europa.eu] European disease agency warns resistant bacteria threaten hospital treatment
items.content_html: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warned on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant bacteria continue to spread across Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatments. Its European Antibiotic Awareness Day alert called for urgent, sustained action. More than 35,000 people die each year from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the European Union and European Economic Area. More than 70% of Europe’s AMR health burden is linked to multidrug-resistant infections acquired in healthcare settings. The ECDC said resistant infections could make it harder or impossible to safely carry out organ transplants, cancer chemotherapy and intensive care. It called for coordinated infection prevention, careful antibiotic prescribing, stronger laboratory capacity and surveillance. Faster genomic monitoring can help track the spread of resistant strains and guide treatment decisions, it said.

items.title: [news-medical.net] Small study links appetite-suppressing drugs to low nutrient intake
items.content_html: A small exploratory study found that some people taking appetite-suppressing medicines such as Wegovy and Mounjaro consumed too little energy and key nutrients and had limited awareness of the potential shortfalls. Researchers asked 14 patients at one English general practice—10 treated privately and four through the National Health Service—to recall what they ate over two days. Average intake was 1,231 calories a day, or 58.5% of estimated energy needs; three participants reported less than 800 calories daily. Participants linked their reduced intake to appetite suppression and described a lack of structured follow-up and dietary advice. Researchers cautioned that the observational study, based on a small group from one relatively affluent practice, cannot establish cause and effect and may not apply widely.

items.title: [frontiersin.org] Kidney studies test earlier detection beyond routine clinical measures
items.content_html: A single-center study of 542 adults with type 2 diabetes found that a model combining routine clinical variables with the TyHGB metabolic index had moderate accuracy in identifying early diabetic kidney disease. The logistic regression model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.709 in a later patient cohort; adding TyHGB did not show a confirmed improvement in that cohort. The researchers said independent, multicenter testing is needed to establish the model’s calibration and clinical usefulness. Two other recent reports examine limits in kidney monitoring. A study of 1,200 cancer patients found that routine estimates of filtration rates could overstate kidney function around critical thresholds, potentially increasing chemotherapy toxicity. A postoperative case series proposes that urine-based biochemical measures may signal recovery from acute kidney injury (AKI) before serum creatinine falls, but calls for larger prospective studies.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
items.content_html: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
items.content_html:
Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles

The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika.

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.

items.title: [gacetamedica.com] Virus treatment improves survival in pancreatic cancer trial; experimental WRN drug shows activity
items.content_html: An international phase 2b trial found that adding the oncolytic virus VCN-01 to chemotherapy increased median overall survival to 10.8 months for patients with previously untreated metastatic pancreatic cancer, compared with 8.6 months for those receiving chemotherapy alone. Madrid’s Hospital 12 de Octubre led the 112-patient trial, and Nature Medicine published the results. A separate phase 1 study tested an experimental WRN inhibitor in advanced solid tumors with microsatellite instability or DNA repair deficiency. Among 66 evaluable patients, 74.2% had disease control and 10.6% had a confirmed partial response. Researchers said the early findings require confirmation in later trials.

items.title: [dailyausaf.com] Studies find Alzheimer’s warning signals years before symptoms emerge
items.content_html: Separate studies report changes in the brain, sleep, navigation and nerve-muscle communication that may appear before Alzheimer’s symptoms, but none establishes a routine early-detection test. A Johns Hopkins team found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala shrank earlier and faster than the hippocampus, with tissue loss in those regions associated with local tau changes. A Stanford-led team used resting-state brain scans to develop an experimental score linked to faster cognitive decline, amyloid buildup and later diagnoses among more than 1,300 initially healthy adults followed for up to 12 years. Other research examined spatial navigation in 100 middle-aged adults at elevated dementia risk. A separate laboratory study found that familial Alzheimer’s mutations disrupted nerve-muscle communication in a model without a brain or spinal cord. A sleep study of 116 adults linked features of deep-sleep waves with cognitive changes over time. The findings come from distinct studies and require further validation; the Stanford score is not available for clinical use, and the nerve-muscle experiment used laboratory models.

items.title: [healio.com] Children with atopic dermatitis show higher odds of sleep disturbance
items.content_html: Children and young adults with atopic dermatitis had 28% higher odds of sleep disturbance than peers without the condition, a retrospective review of 26,395 patients at an urban primary care clinic found. The association remained after researchers accounted for coexisting atopy and mental health conditions; neither significantly changed the link. The study included patients aged 0 to 21; 14.5% had atopic dermatitis and 10.3% had sleep disturbance. Samantha Sundermeier, DO, an attending physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, said future studies should assess disease severity, treatment response and sleep over time using validated measures and patient-reported outcomes.

items.title: [c-jcm.com] Chinese guideline recommends treatments for depression in patients with heart disease
items.content_html: A new multidisciplinary clinical guideline recommends screening for depression and monitoring metabolic health when patients with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease first enter care. It identifies escitalopram and other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors with favorable cardiovascular safety as first-line antidepressants, while advising against tricyclic antidepressants with significant cardiac side effects. The guideline addresses depression's potential two-way links with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease. It also advises clinicians to manage medication interactions that can increase the risk of bleeding or arrhythmia alongside standard heart-disease treatment.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.content_html: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

items.title: [Théoo] My phone is a noisy place
items.content_html:
A while back, I shared a note about how I had cut down my phone usage a lot and what it had changed for me.

And for a few months, I actually stuck to it.
But lately, I've been watching or listening to videos from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep. And for the times when I can't watch videos (like when I'm walking in the street, for example), I will put a podcast or music to occupy the space.

I'm not sure why I went back to this sluggish state when I had been doing so well for a long time, but I think it's because I actually missed watching specific YouTubers and listening to specific podcasts. So I allowed some back into my life and then some more and eventually, it took over.

Which leaves me in a weird situation, because I now know that no YouTube at all is disappointing. There is some content that I actually like and don't want to stop watching, especially since it's only like at most 2 hours per week plus the occasional GeoWizard adventure.
But at the same time, I know that if I let these back in, I won't be able to stop myself, because there is a ton of content that I like, content that I wouldn't miss if I didn't watch it, but that is still nice to watch.
I could try an extension to hide the recommendations, but knowing me, I will probably deactivate it pretty quickly and find an "acceptable" reason why. Worth a try though, I guess.

The other thing that crept back is Spotify. I listen to music (or podcasts, but mostly music) when I'm not watching videos. On the one hand, it's great because I have discovered many new artists lately, but at the same time, I've been feeling more disconnected, irritated when someone is trying to talk to me and I have to remove my AirPods and, overall like my mind can never breathe.
I'd say that the thing that has changed since the last article is that now silence isn't weird anymore. I even enjoy it! But for some reason I always feel this need to listen to something. Plus, I have been questioning my relationship with music lately, but I will talk about it in another note.

Now again, I'm not sure about what the right thing to do is. I definitely don't want to stop listening to music, I enjoy it way too much. But I don't want it to be constant.
Trying to apply time restrictions won't work because I know that I will find "good reasons" to circumvent them.
Maybe something like "you can only listen to music when you do this and that" could work. This has worked for podcasts already, as there are some podcasts that I only listen to when cleaning and others I only listen to when grocery shopping.
Another idea would be to say "You can only listen to music out loud" and not in your AirPods. So that would automatically limit my time, because there are many situations where you can't listen to music out loud.

So where does this leave me? What about the things I said in the previous note about enjoying life without all this?
I guess it's as with all things in life, I need to find balance.

The approach to ditch all music and YouTube was certainly too extreme, but spending my whole days listening to stuff is also too extreme.
Another thing to consider is the fact that I tend to get absorbed by things, both the good and the bad ones.
So when I get to reading a book or programming something, I will just do it for hours upon hours to the point of forgetting to eat. But the same can be said for playing video games and watching videos, which has a much more negative impact.
And I don't know that I should change this, it's just a part of my personality, but I need to learn to put systems in place to prevent it for things that make me rot away.

I don't have a good conclusion yet. Honestly, I think that what would help me would be to have the opinions from a bunch of different people and see how they deal with all this, to try as many options as possible until I find the balance I'm looking for.

For now, I will try to limit Spotify and I will try YouTube "blocking" extensions. If you have any other ideas or want to share your experience, please email me, I'd be grateful to receive it.

I hope you have a great day, bye.

It reveals little about an individual’s body composition—is the weight fat or muscle, for example?—and perhaps most importantly, it says little about whether excess body fat is actually affecting a person’s health. items.title: [ScienceDaily] A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome
items.content_html: Scientists have developed a promising new fiber supplement that improves gut health in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) without worsening bloating, pain, or other digestive symptoms. The specially designed blend also improved gut-related anxiety and produced surprisingly rapid changes in gut bacteria, potentially offering a new way to manage IBS.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis
items.content_html: A new study suggests that the right kind of exercise could help protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery. Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life without damaging knee cartilage. The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.

items.title: [techxplore.com] Microsoft outage exposed server-health failures across cloud workplace systems
items.content_html: Microsoft’s investigation into its global Microsoft 365 outage points to backend servers that failed automated health checks, leaving the remaining systems struggling with heavier traffic. Engineers’ attempts to restart servers also failed when traffic returned, while a later network change exposed a problem introduced during an earlier capacity upgrade. The failure disrupted Exchange Online, Microsoft’s cloud email and scheduling service, and affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot across government, business and public services. Microsoft said neither a cyberattack nor artificial-intelligence agents caused the incident. Engineers gradually restored services while working through an email backlog. Digital Trends reported that engineers deployed a patch targeting an authentication and routing component. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the company would publish a review with a step-by-step timeline and repair measures. Microsoft’s notice to customers said it would issue a preliminary report within two business days and a final report within five.
